newsitem.title: UK: DMG seen continuing investment bank drive.
newsitem.headline: DMG seen continuing investment bank drive.

text.p: High-profile problems within its asset management arm will not dent Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's plans for expansion, banking analysts said on Thursday.

"They will continue to expand in investment banking. They still have a couple of gaps to fill. But they may be a bit more cautious than they were before," an analyst at a European investment bank told Reuters.

Fund arm Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), last year rocked by revelations of misvaluations in three of its funds and the subsequent sacking of fund manager Peter Young, is now embroiled in a dispute with top fund manager Nicola Horlick.

Investment banks are scrambling to make inroads into the lucrative area of asset management and the analyst, who wished to remain anonymous, said this will continue to be a priority for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG), despite its recent difficulties.

"They still believe asset management to be one of the main growth areas going forward," he said, adding that if the price was right it would probably grow this part of its business through acquisitions.
But concerns that pension funds might move elsewhere did leave a question mark hanging over how viable this might be.

"It definitely poses questions for the future prospects of this part of the business. Nicola Horlick was instrumental in its performance," said one banking source, pointing out that compound growth for MGAM between 1992 and 1996 was 25 percent.
"The UK pension fund business has enjoyed even faster growth of more than 30 percent," he added.
On Wednesday, the Merchant Navy Officer's Pension Fund, which has around 50 million pounds invested at MGAM, was reported to have said it was worried about Horlick's sudden suspension.
And other clients, including London's Westminster City Council, are reviewing their relationship with MGAM following the Young scandal.

The Railway Pension Trustee Company, which has 1.25 billion pounds invested with MGAM, said it had met MGAM officials and would be in close contact with its asset managers over the coming months. This should not, however, have an impact on other areas where DMG, the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank, has said it needs to grow. This includes its British brokerage side, where it still has to hire traders and analysts, as part of an expansion into European equities.
Horlick was suspended on Tuesday pending the outcome of an internal investigation into what Deutsche Morgan Grenfell described as "a potential breach of her contract".
The dispute is believed to revolve around allegations that Horlick tried to take a number of her MGAM team with her in a move to rival firm Dutch bank ABN AMRO.

Horlick's suspension comes when MGAM is still awaiting the outcome of a probe into the Young affair which is widely expected to lead to a hefty fine from the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO).

And Deutsche, which has already had to inject 180 million pounds into the funds and faces a compensation bill of another 200 million pounds as well as a large bill for fees and costs, last month lost its coveted triple-A credit rating from Moody's.
This could have a negative impact on its funding operations, particularly swaps and derivatives.
While this combination of factors may mean DMG has to control its expansion more carefully than over the last two years, analysts said the firm has learned a lot.
It will put this experience to good use, but events in London will almost certainly mean firmer control from Deutsche's headquarters in Frankfurt.
"Frankfurt is more in control than it was before," the first analyst said.
